subtype: Stage 4: Consequences and loss of control [Actor]
passage:
Jyoti had promised Maa on Chhath morning, her hand on his head: no more drinking. He meant it. He lasted four days. By the fifth evening the pull was louder than the promise, and he was behind the grain godown with the older boys again.
Now the consequences kept coming. His B.Com marks sheet from the college in Siwan showed two backlogs. Rehana, who ran the tuition centre where he taught maths in the evenings, had called him in on Monday. "Late three times, and once you smelt of it in front of the children. I can't keep you, Jyoti." He had nodded, face hot, unable to argue.
Tonight he sat on the canal bridge with an empty bottle at his feet, counting the promises he'd broken this year. He had tried cutting down to weekends, then to festivals only. Every plan had lasted less than a week. He felt like a rat in a drum, running and getting nowhere.

qa.q: How many backlogs did Jyoti's B.Com marks sheet show?
How does Jyoti feel on the canal bridge, and what shows it?
qa.a: He feels ashamed and trapped; he counts his broken promises and feels like a rat in a drum, running and getting nowhere.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Jyoti at this stage?
qa.a: Since cutting down alone keeps failing, he could tell Maa the whole truth and go with her to a doctor or de-addiction centre for proper help.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Rehana to let Jyoti go?
qa.a: Rehana had to protect the children, but letting go of a teacher who came late and smelt of alcohol may have felt sad and uncomfortable, especially seeing him unable to argue.

grounding: Shows a young man's drinking costing him marks and a job, failed attempts to cut down, and a sincere promise to his mother broken within days.

subtype: Stage 4: Consequences and loss of control [Actor]
passage:
Zanele had set the timer for two hours. She had set it every night that week, and every night she had switched it off and played on until the birds started in the jacaranda outside her Johannesburg residence window.
Now the consequences were arriving all at once. An email from her tutor: three missed tutorials, final warning. A bookshop shift lost because she slept through it. And Omar on the phone that afternoon, tired rather than angry: "I don't know how to be with someone who's always somewhere else."
At Easter she had promised her mother, crying, that this term would be different. She had meant every word.
Tonight she deleted the game, then sat on her bed for twenty minutes before reinstalling it, hating herself the whole time. The shame only made her want to disappear into it more.

qa.q: How long did Zanele set the timer for each night?
Why did Zanele reinstall the game while hating herself?
qa.a: The craving was stronger than her sincere wish to stop, and the shame of failing again made her want to escape into the game even more.

qa.q: What could Zanele do now that cutting down on her own keeps failing?
qa.a: She could tell someone safe, like her mother or Omar, and reach out to the university counselling service or a doctor for proper help instead of relying on timers.

qa.q: What is Omar experiencing in the relationship right now?
qa.a: Omar sounds tired rather than angry, feeling alone because Zanele is 'always somewhere else' and unsure how to stay close.

grounding: Illustrates gaming costing a student her tutorials, a job shift and closeness in a relationship, with failed cut-downs and a broken promise to her mother.
